title: Theodicy: God, Evil and Suffering
subtitle: If God is good and powerful, why is there so much evil and pain? The question, the Bible's own answers and protests, the main Christian and Jewish responses, and how to stay with people who suffer
plain: Theodicy is the attempt to show that God is just and good even though the world is full of evil and suffering; a 'defence' aims at less, showing only that God and evil are not logically contradictory. The problem is ancient and sharp: if God is fully good, fully powerful and fully knowing, why does he allow children to die of cancer, tsunamis to drown villages and people to torture one another? The Bible does not hide from this question. It contains whole books of protest (Job, Lamentations, Habakkuk), prayers that accuse God (Ps 88), and Jesus himself crying 'My God, why have you forsaken me?' (Mark 15:34). Christians and Jews have given many serious answers: evil comes from misused freedom, suffering can grow souls, God has reasons we cannot see, the world is a battlefield with real enemies, God suffers with us on the cross, and God will finally wipe away every tear (Rev 21:4). No answer removes all the difficulty, and the Bible itself warns against neat explanations offered to people in pain (Job 42:7). Most wise teachers hold the explanations loosely and the sufferer closely: lament, presence and hope come first, arguments second.
keyPoints: The problem is usually stated as an 'inconsistent triad': God is all-powerful, God is wholly good, and evil exists. Every response either denies that the three really conflict or adjusts how one of them is understood.

Philosophers separate the logical problem (God and evil cannot both exist) from the evidential problem (the amount and kind of evil make God unlikely). Many philosophers, including many atheists, think Alvin Plantinga's free-will defence answered the logical form; the evidential form, pressed by William Rowe in 1979, is still widely debated.

The Bible rejects the simple rule that suffering always proves sin: God rebukes Job's friends (Job 42:7) and Jesus denies that the man born blind or the victims at Siloam were worse sinners (John 9:1-3, Luke 13:1-5).

Lament is not a lack of faith. About a third of the Psalms are complaints addressed to God, and the tradition of arguing with God runs from Abraham (Gen 18:25) and Moses (Exod 32:11-14) to Jewish thinkers after the Holocaust.

The main Christian responses (Augustinian, soul-making, free will, Reformed sovereignty, cosmic conflict, skeptical theism, open theism, process, cruciform) disagree about God's power, knowledge and control. Each has real strengths and real costs.

The New Testament answer is less an explanation than a story: God enters suffering in Jesus, defeats evil through the cross and resurrection, and promises a renewed creation where death is no more (Rom 8:18-25, 1 Cor 15:26, Rev 21:1-5).
Related problems include divine hiddenness, hell, violence in the Old Testament and animal suffering before humans existed; each sharpens the main question in a different way.

Pastorally, presence comes before explanation. Job's friends did best in their first seven silent days (Job 2:13). 'Everything happens for a reason' and 'you must not have enough faith' wound people and are not biblical teaching.

map.title: The map of the problem of evil
map.intro: Start with the triad in the centre. Red-toned nodes state the problem in its different forms; the others are the main responses from Scripture, Christian tradition, philosophy and Jewish thought. Follow the arrows to see what answers what, what grows out of what, and where views clash. No single node is 'the answer'; most thoughtful believers combine several.

nodes.label: The inconsistent triad
nodes.detail: Three claims that seem unable to be true together: God is all-powerful, God is perfectly good, and evil exists. Lactantius reports Epicurus framing it this way, and David Hume restated it. Every theodicy is an attempt to show the three are consistent, or to refine what one of them means.

nodes.label: Logical problem
nodes.detail: The claim that God and evil are strictly contradictory, so belief in God is irrational. J. L. Mackie pressed this in 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955). The argument needs a hidden premise: that a good, powerful God would always eliminate evil. Critics of the argument ask whether that premise is necessarily true.

nodes.label: Evidential problem
nodes.detail: The weaker but stronger-feeling claim: the amount and kind of evil make God's existence improbable. William Rowe (1979) imagined a fawn trapped in a forest fire, burned and dying for days with no one to see it. Such suffering seems pointless, and a good God would not allow pointless suffering.

nodes.label: Moral evil
nodes.detail: Evil done by free agents: murder, cruelty, injustice, abuse, war. The Bible traces it to the human heart and to the misuse of the freedom God gave (Gen 4:6-8, Jer 17:9). It is the easiest kind to connect to the free-will response.

nodes.label: Natural evil
nodes.detail: Suffering that no human chose: earthquakes, tsunamis, disease, birth defects, famine. It is harder to blame on human freedom. Responses link it to the Fall, to fixed natural laws, to fallen spiritual powers, or to a creation that is good but not yet finished.

nodes.label: Gratuitous evil
nodes.detail: Evil that serves no greater good at all. If even one such evil exists, many argue, God cannot be both good and powerful. Theists either deny that any evil is truly pointless (skeptical theism, Reformed view) or argue that God may permit some pointless evil as the cost of a world with real freedom and stable laws (open theism, some free-will views).

nodes.label: Horrendous evils
nodes.detail: Marilyn McCord Adams' term for evils so terrible that they seem to destroy the meaning of a person's life, such as a parent forced to harm their own child. She argued that general 'greater good' arguments are not enough; God must defeat such evils within each victim's own life, finally through union with God.

nodes.label: Divine hiddenness
nodes.detail: A related problem: if a loving God exists, why do many sincere seekers find no sign of him? J. L. Schellenberg argued in 1993 that a perfectly loving God would always make a relationship available to anyone not resisting it. The Bible itself speaks of God hiding his face.

nodes.label: Animal and pre-human suffering
nodes.detail: Fossils show predation, disease and extinction for millions of years before humans. This troubles theodicies that blame all suffering on human sin. Responses include a cosmic fall of angelic powers, a 'cost of an evolving world' view, or a reading of Genesis in which death among animals was not the 'death' brought by sin.

nodes.label: The book of Job
nodes.detail: A blameless man loses everything after the accuser questions his motives. His friends insist he must have sinned; Job protests his innocence and demands a hearing. God answers from the whirlwind with questions about creation, never explaining the heavenly wager, then says the friends were wrong and Job spoke rightly.

nodes.label: Lament and protest prayer
nodes.detail: The Bible gives sufferers words to complain to God: 'How long, O Lord?' (Ps 13:1). Lament is covenant speech: it holds God to his promises. Ps 88 ends in darkness without resolution, which tells sufferers that even unresolved prayer belongs in Scripture.

nodes.label: Retribution theology
nodes.detail: The principle that the righteous prosper and the wicked suffer. It is true as a covenant pattern (Deut 28) and in Proverbs, but Job, Ecclesiastes and Jesus deny that it works as a rule for reading individual lives. Misused, it becomes the idea that every sufferer deserves it.

nodes.label: Jesus on suffering
nodes.detail: Jesus refuses to link specific disasters to specific sins (Luke 13:1-5, John 9:1-3). He weeps at a tomb (John 11:35), heals as a sign of God's kingdom pushing back evil (Luke 13:16), and calls all people to repentance in the face of life's fragility.

nodes.label: The cross
nodes.detail: For Christians, the centre of any answer. The worst moral evil in the story, the murder of the innocent Son, is both freely done by wicked people and within God's saving plan (Acts 2:23). On the cross God does not explain suffering from a distance but enters it.

nodes.label: Eschatological hope
nodes.detail: The promise that present suffering is not the last word. Creation groans like a woman in labour waiting for renewal (Rom 8:18-25). Death will be destroyed (1 Cor 15:26) and God will wipe every tear (Rev 21:4). Many think no theodicy works without this horizon.

nodes.label: Augustinian: privation and Fall
nodes.detail: Augustine taught that God made everything good and that evil is not a 'thing' but a lack or twisting of good, like blindness in an eye. Evil entered through the free rebellion of angels and humans; natural disorder follows the Fall. God permits evil only because he can bring greater good out of it.

nodes.label: Irenaean soul-making
nodes.detail: Following hints in Irenaeus, John Hick (1966) argued that humans were made immature and placed in a challenging world at an 'epistemic distance' from God, so that they could freely grow into children of God. A world without pain could not produce courage, compassion or trust.

nodes.label: Free-will defence
nodes.detail: Alvin Plantinga argued that a world with creatures who are truly free to do good is more valuable than a world of puppets, and that it is possible even God could not create such a world without some of them choosing evil. If that is even possible, the logical problem fails.

nodes.label: Reformed meticulous sovereignty
nodes.detail: God ordains everything that happens, including evil acts, without himself doing evil; human agents remain responsible (compatibilism). Joseph's words are the key text: 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good' (Gen 50:20). Evil is never pointless because God has a good purpose for every event.

nodes.label: Best of all possible worlds
nodes.detail: Gottfried Leibniz, who coined the word 'theodicy' (1710), argued that a perfect God must create the best possible world, so this one, with its evils, is the best whole. After the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 Voltaire mocked the idea in *Candide*.

nodes.label: Cosmic conflict / warfare
nodes.detail: The world is a battlefield. Real spiritual powers who freely rebelled against God oppress creation, and Jesus came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8). Much evil is not God's will at all but the work of enemies whose defeat began at the cross. Greg Boyd is a leading modern voice.

nodes.label: Skeptical theism
nodes.detail: If God exists, we should expect not to see many of his reasons, just as an infant cannot see the reasons for a vaccination. So 'I cannot see a reason' does not show 'there is no reason'. Stephen Wykstra (1984) and Michael Bergmann developed this as a reply to Rowe.

nodes.label: Open theism
nodes.detail: God knows everything that can be known, but the future free choices of creatures are not yet settled and so not yet knowable. God takes real risks in creating free beings. Specific evils may be genuinely pointless and grieve God, who works to bring good out of them.

nodes.label: Process theology
nodes.detail: God's power is persuasive, not coercive. God cannot unilaterally stop evil, because every creature has some power of its own. God lures the world toward good and suffers with it. This removes the problem of why God does not intervene, at the cost of a much more limited God.

nodes.label: Theology of the cross
nodes.detail: Luther taught that God is known most truly in weakness and suffering, not in displays of glory. Jürgen Moltmann (*The Crucified God*, 1972) argued that God himself suffers the godforsakenness of the cross. The answer to suffering is a suffering God who shares it from inside and overcomes it.

nodes.label: Can God suffer?
nodes.detail: Classical theology (impassibility) says God is not overwhelmed or changed by suffering; the Son suffered in his human nature. Many modern theologians (passibility) say a loving God must truly feel grief. Both sides affirm that in Christ God truly entered human suffering.

nodes.label: Protest: Ivan Karamazov
nodes.detail: In Dostoevsky's novel (1880), Ivan does not deny God; he refuses the deal. No future harmony could justify the tears of one tortured child, so he 'returns his ticket'. Dostoevsky answers not with an argument but with the life of Father Zosima and Alyosha's active love.

nodes.label: Arguing with God
nodes.detail: A deep Jewish tradition of holding God to his own justice. Abraham asks, 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?' (Gen 18:25). Moses pleads against God's wrath. Rabbinic stories, Yiddish prayers and Wiesel's *The Trial of God* continue it. Protest is an act of faith in God's covenant, not a rejection of it.

nodes.label: Post-Holocaust theology
nodes.detail: After six million Jews were murdered, Jewish thinkers divided. Richard Rubenstein rejected the God who acts in history; Emil Fackenheim named a '614th commandment' not to give Hitler posthumous victories; Eliezer Berkovits spoke of God hiding his face; Hans Jonas proposed a God who gave up power. Elie Wiesel kept faith and protest together.

nodes.label: Kushner: good but limited
nodes.detail: Rabbi Harold Kushner, after his son died of a rare ageing disease, wrote *When Bad Things Happen to Good People* (1981). He concluded that God is good but does not control everything; God does not send tragedy but gives strength to bear it. The book comforted millions and was criticised for shrinking God.

nodes.label: Presence before explanation
nodes.detail: Most pastoral wisdom says: sit with sufferers, weep with them, and do not hurry to explain. Job's friends were wise for seven silent days and foolish once they started to explain. Paul says God comforts us so we can comfort others.
examples: Nicholas Wolterstorff, Lament for a Son

nodes.label: Karma and grace
nodes.detail: In India, suffering is often explained by karma: the results of deeds in this or past lives. This resembles the retribution theology of Job's friends. The gospel answer stresses grace: suffering is not a simple payment for past deeds, and God's mercy is not earned. Christians should speak of this respectfully, knowing that Hindu traditions also teach grace (for example in Tamil Saiva and Vaishnava devotion).

flow.title: Walking through evil and suffering: a path for thinking and praying
flow.intro: Use this path when you face a real evil, your own or someone else's, or when you study a hard passage about suffering. The order matters: it moves from honesty, to prayer, to careful thought, to action and hope. Many people jump straight to step 7 (explanations) and skip the rest; the Bible does not.

steps.label: Name the evil honestly
steps.detail: Say plainly what happened and that it is wrong. The Bible never calls evil good. Jesus was 'deeply moved' and angry at death before he raised Lazarus. Do not rush to soften the harm with religious phrases.
ask: What exactly happened, and who was harmed?
Am I tempted to say it was 'not so bad' to protect God or myself?
What would I call this if it happened to a stranger?

steps.label: Identify the kind of evil
steps.detail: Is this moral evil (someone chose it), natural evil (disease, disaster), or both? Is it horrendous, the kind that threatens to destroy a life's meaning? Different responses fit different kinds, and mixing them up causes harm, for example blaming a cancer patient for their illness.
ask: Did a human or group choose this, or did it come through nature?
Is there injustice here that needs to be named and resisted?
Does this evil seem to have any possible good outcome, or does it seem pointless?

steps.label: Separate the two questions
steps.detail: There is the intellectual question ('How can God allow this?') and the personal one ('Where is God for me now?'). C. S. Lewis wrote one book on each: *The Problem of Pain* (1940) and, after his wife died, *A Grief Observed* (1961). A grieving person usually needs the second kind of help first.
ask: Is the person asking for an argument, or for help to survive?
Am I answering a question that was not asked?
What does the sufferer need from me today?

steps.label: Bring it to God in lament
steps.detail: Biblical lament usually has a shape: address God, complain honestly, ask for help, state trust, and sometimes promise praise. But Ps 88 has almost none of that and is still Scripture. You are allowed to say 'How long?' and 'Why?'. This is covenant faith speaking, not unbelief.
ask: What do I actually want to say to God, without editing?
Which psalm says what I feel (Ps 13, 22, 44, 88)?
Can I keep talking to God even if I am angry with him?

steps.label: Test every explanation against Scripture
steps.detail: Ask whether an explanation repeats the mistake of Job's friends: assuming suffering proves sin, or that God owes success to the faithful. Jesus rejects that reasoning. Also ask whether it makes God the author of sin, or so weak that he cannot save.
ask: Does this explanation blame the victim?
Would God say of this explanation what he said to Eliphaz (Job 42:7)?
Does it fit the character of God shown in Jesus?
Does it still let me call evil evil?

steps.label: Look at the cross
steps.detail: The cross does not explain every evil, but it shows three things: God is not distant from suffering; God can bring salvation through the worst evil without approving it; and evil does not have the last word. Christians read every other suffering in that light.
ask: What does it mean that God's Son cried 'why have you forsaken me'?
How can the cross be both a great crime and God's plan (Acts 2:23)?
What does the resurrection say about this situation?

steps.label: Weigh the main responses
steps.detail: Now compare the theodicies: free will, soul-making, sovereignty, cosmic conflict, skeptical theism, and others. Ask what each says about this specific evil. Most wise believers draw on several and admit that some mystery remains.
ask: Which response best explains this kind of evil?
What does each response cost (God's power, goodness, or our understanding)?
Where must I say 'I do not know'?

steps.label: Act against the evil
steps.detail: The Bible's main response to evil is not a theory but resistance: heal, feed, protect, seek justice, forgive. Jesus treated sickness and oppression as enemies to defeat. Theodicy that leads to passivity has gone wrong.
ask: What practical help is needed now?
Is there an injustice I should oppose?
Where can my own suffering make me more able to comfort others?

steps.label: Hold on to hope
steps.detail: The final answer in Scripture is the renewal of all things. Paul does not call present suffering small; he says it is not worth comparing with the glory to come. Hope does not cancel grief; it lets us 'grieve, but not as those who have no hope'.
ask: What does God promise about the end of this suffering?
How do Rom 8 and Rev 21 change how I see today?
Who can hold hope for me when I cannot hold it myself?

decision.title: Which response to evil fits your convictions?
decision.intro: This tree helps you see where your existing beliefs about God and the world lead. It does not tell you which view is true. If you are in pain right now, take the first branch; the arguments can wait.

nodes.q: What brings you to this question right now?

options.label: I or someone close to me is suffering now
I want to think through the intellectual problem
I am troubled by a specific Bible passage or event

nodes.q: What do you need most at this moment?

options.label: Words to speak to God, even angry ones
To know God is with me in this
To know this will not last forever

nodes.q: What kind of text troubles you?

options.label: A text where God seems to send disaster or evil (Isa 45:7, Amos 3:6)
A text that says the righteous always prosper
Violence commanded in the Old Testament

nodes.q: Does God decide every event that happens, including each evil act?

options.label: Yes: nothing happens outside God's specific plan
No: God allows creatures real freedom that he does not control
I am not sure

nodes.q: Then does God have a good purpose for every evil, even if we cannot see it?

options.label: Yes, and Scripture shows enough of it to trust him
Yes, but we usually cannot see it at all

nodes.q: Does God know every future free choice before it happens?

options.label: Yes, God knows the whole future
No, the free future is open and not yet knowable

nodes.q: Why did God give freedom that leads to evil?

options.label: Because love and goodness require real freedom
Because character is formed by struggle
Because spiritual powers also have freedom, and they rebelled

nodes.q: Could God stop any evil he wanted to stop, if he chose to?

options.label: Yes, God is all-powerful
No, God's power is persuasive, not controlling
I cannot answer, and I want to protest

results.title: Start with lament
results.text: Pray the lament psalms out loud: Ps 13 if you feel forgotten, Ps 22 if you feel abandoned, Ps 44 if you feel faithful yet punished, Ps 88 if you have no words of hope left. The Bible gives you permission to complain to God. Find one person who will listen without explaining.

results.title: The God who suffers with you
results.text: Christians believe God has been inside human suffering in Jesus: rejected, tortured, abandoned, killed. He does not ask you to suffer anything he refused to share. Read the passion story slowly, and the promise that we have a high priest who sympathises with our weakness. This is the heart of the theology of the cross.

results.title: Eschatological hope
results.text: Scripture promises a day when God will wipe away every tear and death will be no more. Paul, who suffered greatly, calls present troubles 'light and momentary' only when compared with that coming glory. Hope does not deny grief; it holds it within a larger story.

results.title: Let wisdom books correct each other
results.text: Proverbs gives general patterns (wise living tends to go well). Job and Ecclesiastes show the exceptions: the righteous can suffer and the wicked can prosper. The Bible holds these together on purpose. Read Prov 3 alongside Job 21 and Ps 73.

results.title: See the course lesson on hard texts
results.text: Violence in the Old Testament is a related but separate problem. The app's course lesson [Hard Texts: Violence, Accommodation and Changing Perception](/course/hard-texts) sets out the main ways of reading these passages (hyperbole in ancient war language, accommodation, progressive revelation, the Jesus lens) and their critiques.

results.title: Reformed / meticulous sovereignty
results.text: Your answers fit the Reformed view (Calvin, Westminster Confession, D. A. Carson, John Piper): God ordains all things, including evil acts, for good ends, while humans remain responsible and God is not the author of sin. Its comfort is that no suffering is wasted. Its hardest question is how God is not responsible for evil he decrees. Read the critiques of this view as well.

results.title: Skeptical theism
results.text: Your answers fit skeptical theism (Stephen Wykstra, Michael Bergmann): the gap between God's mind and ours means we should not expect to see God's reasons. This is a defence, not a full theodicy. Critics say it makes it hard to judge anything as good or bad. It is held both by Reformed and non-Reformed thinkers.

results.title: Open theism
results.text: Your answers fit open theism (Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, William Hasker, Greg Boyd): God created a world with a genuinely open future, took a risk, and does not plan each evil. Some evils are truly pointless and grieve God. Its strength is that God is never the author of a child's murder. Critics say it weakens God's knowledge and the certainty of his promises.

results.title: Free-will theodicy
results.text: Your answers fit the free-will response (Augustine in its roots, Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne): God values creatures who can freely love, and freedom makes evil possible. It explains moral evil well. Its weak points are natural evil and the sheer scale of some evils. Many combine it with soul-making or cosmic conflict to cover those.

results.title: Irenaean soul-making
results.text: Your answers fit the soul-making view (Irenaeus, John Hick): the world is a place where humans grow from innocence to maturity. Pain makes courage, compassion and faith possible. Critics ask why some suffering crushes rather than grows people, and why infants and animals suffer.

results.title: Cosmic conflict (warfare) theodicy
results.text: Your answers fit the warfare view (many church fathers, C. S. Lewis in parts, Greg Boyd): the world is in a war zone. Rebellious spiritual powers corrupt creation, and Jesus' ministry and cross are God's counter-attack. It explains why Jesus treated disease as an enemy. Critics say it is hard to prove and can make Satan too strong.

results.title: Process theology
results.text: Your answers fit process theology (Whitehead, Hartshorne, David Ray Griffin) or the related 'essential kenosis' view (Thomas Jay Oord): God cannot force outcomes but lures the world toward good and suffers with it. It removes the question 'why did God not stop it?'. Critics say it gives up the biblical Creator and any guarantee that evil will be defeated.

results.title: The protest tradition
results.text: Your answer fits the biblical and Jewish tradition of arguing with God: Abraham, Moses, Job, Jeremiah, and after the Holocaust Elie Wiesel. Protest takes God's justice so seriously that it holds God to it. It is a form of faith. Many in this tradition never resolve the question and still pray.

timeline.title: How people have wrestled with evil and God

events.label: Lament psalms collected
events.text: Many lament psalms are attributed to David and his musicians, though the Psalter was gathered over centuries. They give Israel a worship language for complaint, from 'How long?' (Ps 13) to the unrelieved darkness of Ps 88. Dates of individual psalms are debated.

events.label: Habakkuk argues with God
events.text: As Babylon rises, Habakkuk asks why God lets the wicked swallow the righteous (Hab 1:13). God answers that the righteous will live by faithfulness (Hab 2:4). The prophet ends trusting God even with empty fields (Hab 3:17-19). Date approximate.

events.label: Jerusalem falls; Lamentations
events.text: The Babylonians destroy the temple. Lamentations mourns the city in five acrostic poems, admits sin, and also protests the horror (Lam 2:20). At its centre stands hope in God's steadfast love (Lam 3:22-23). It ends with an open question (Lam 5:20-22).

events.label: Job takes final shape
events.text: The date of the book of Job is unknown; many scholars place its final form between the 7th and 4th centuries BC, while its setting is patriarchal. It is the Bible's longest treatment of innocent suffering.

events.label: Epicurus' dilemma
events.text: The Greek philosopher Epicurus (died about 270 BC) is credited with the dilemma: either God wants to remove evil and cannot, or can and does not want to. The form we know comes from the Christian writer Lactantius, centuries later.

events.label: Jesus on Siloam and the blind man
events.text: Jesus rejects the idea that victims of a collapsed tower or a man born blind suffered for special sins (Luke 13:1-5, John 9:1-3). Within a few years he is crucified, crying the words of Ps 22. Exact year debated (about AD 30 or 33).

events.label: Paul writes Romans 8
events.text: Paul describes creation groaning in labour pains, the Spirit groaning in prayer, and nothing able to separate believers from God's love (Rom 8:18-39). Date approximate.

events.label: Irenaeus on growth
events.text: In *Against Heresies* Irenaeus pictures humans created as children who must grow into maturity and likeness to God. John Hick later took this as the seed of 'soul-making' theodicy. Date approximate.

events.label: Lactantius records the dilemma
events.text: In *On the Anger of God* (chapter 13), Lactantius reports Epicurus' argument and answers that God permits evil so that wisdom and virtue can exist. Date approximate.

events.label: Augustine's Enchiridion
events.text: Augustine sums up his view: evil is the privation (absence) of good, entering by the free will of angels and humans, and God, being good, would not allow evil unless he could bring good out of it. Western theology followed him for a thousand years. Date approximate.

events.label: Aquinas' Summa begins
events.text: Thomas Aquinas places the problem of evil as the first objection to God's existence and answers, following Augustine, that God permits evil to bring good out of it. He develops evil as privation and God as impassible.

events.label: Luther's theology of the cross
events.text: At the Heidelberg Disputation, Luther contrasts a 'theologian of glory', who calls evil good, with a 'theologian of the cross', who calls a thing what it is and finds God hidden in suffering.

events.label: Leibniz coins 'theodicy'
events.text: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz publishes *Essais de Théodicée*, from Greek words for 'God' and 'justice'. He argues that God chose the best of all possible worlds.

events.label: Lisbon earthquake
events.text: On 1 November, All Saints' Day, an earthquake, tsunami and fires destroy Lisbon, killing tens of thousands, many in churches. European thinkers debate whether this can be 'the best of all possible worlds'. Voltaire writes a poem (1756) and *Candide* (1759).

events.label: Hume's Dialogues published
events.text: In David Hume's *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*, published after his death, the character Philo restates 'Epicurus's old questions' and argues that the world's mixed goodness does not point to a perfectly good designer.

events.label: The Brothers Karamazov
events.text: Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov tells stories of tortured children and refuses any harmony bought at that price. Dostoevsky answers through the characters of Zosima and Alyosha rather than an argument.

events.label: Mackie's logical argument
events.text: J. L. Mackie's article 'Evil and Omnipotence' argues that the beliefs of theists are positively irrational. It sets the agenda for twenty years of philosophy of religion.

events.label: Wiesel's Night in English
events.text: Elie Wiesel's memoir of Auschwitz and Buchenwald appears in English (Yiddish 1956, French 1958). It records the death of faith in a God of easy answers and the question 'Where is God?' at the hanging of a child.

events.label: Hick and Rubenstein
events.text: John Hick publishes *Evil and the God of Love*, setting Augustinian and Irenaean theodicies side by side. Richard Rubenstein publishes *After Auschwitz*, rejecting the traditional God of history. Emil Fackenheim announces his '614th commandment' the following year (1967).

events.label: Moltmann's The Crucified God
events.text: Jürgen Moltmann argues that God suffers in the cross of Jesus and that only a suffering God can help. The book shapes modern theology of suffering (English 1974).

events.label: Plantinga's free-will defence
events.text: Alvin Plantinga's *God, Freedom and Evil* argues that it is possible God could not create free creatures who never do wrong. Many philosophers come to regard the logical problem as answered.

events.label: Rowe's evidential argument
events.text: William Rowe's paper with the dying fawn shifts debate to the evidential problem: intense suffering that seems pointless makes God unlikely. Stephen Wykstra replies in 1984 with what becomes skeptical theism.

events.label: Kushner's best-seller
events.text: Rabbi Harold Kushner's *When Bad Things Happen to Good People* argues that God does not cause tragedies and is not all-controlling. Millions of readers, Jewish and Christian, find comfort; many theologians object.

events.label: Indian Ocean tsunami
events.text: On 26 December, a tsunami kills about 230,000 people across many countries, including thousands on the Tamil Nadu coast, especially Nagapattinam district. Christians, Hindus and Muslims ask why; churches and temples become relief centres. Many Christian leaders said publicly that the first responses must be grief, presence and practical help, not quick explanations.

gallery.title: Texts, thinkers and events in the conversation
gallery.intro: Filter by colour group to see the biblical texts, the classic and modern thinkers, the Jewish voices, and the events and lives that shaped how people think about evil. Each card says what the person or text contributes and where it is questioned.

items.title: Job
items.summary: A blameless man suffers, argues with God and is finally answered from the whirlwind.
items.detail: The prologue lets readers see what Job never sees: a heavenly scene in which 'the satan' (Hebrew ha-satan, 'the accuser', with the article, more a title than a name) questions whether Job serves God for nothing. Job's friends defend God by accusing Job. Job accuses God but keeps addressing him. God's speeches (Job 38-41) do not explain the suffering; they widen Job's view of a vast, wild creation that God governs. God then says the friends 'have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has' (Job 42:7) and asks Job to pray for them. Readers disagree whether the restoration at the end (Job 42:10-17) undercuts or completes the book's message.

items.title: Psalm 88: the darkest psalm
items.summary: A lament that never turns to praise and ends with the word 'darkness'.
items.detail: Most laments move from complaint to trust. Psalm 88 does not. The psalmist has been afflicted since youth, feels cut off from God, and ends with friends gone and darkness as the only companion. Yet the whole psalm is addressed to 'the God of my salvation' (Ps 88:1). Its place in the Bible tells sufferers that continuing to pray in the dark is itself faith.

items.title: Psalm 22: forsaken and rescued
items.summary: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?', the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross.
items.detail: The psalm alternates between abandonment and remembered trust, then turns to praise as God answers (Ps 22:21-24) and ends with the nations worshipping. When Jesus quotes its first line (Mark 15:34), Jewish hearers who knew the psalm by its opening would hear both the cry and the whole arc. Jesus' cry was real anguish, not a performance.

items.title: Psalm 44: faithful yet crushed
items.summary: The nation protests that it suffers even though it has kept the covenant.
items.detail: Israel recalls God's past victories, then says: 'All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you' (Ps 44:17). It rejects the idea that the disaster is punishment and calls God to 'wake up' (Ps 44:23). Paul quotes verse 22 in Rom 8:36. Jewish thinkers after the Holocaust have often turned to this psalm.

items.title: Psalm 73: the prosperity of the wicked
items.summary: Asaph nearly loses faith watching the wicked thrive, until he enters God's sanctuary.
items.detail: The psalm honestly states the problem (Ps 73:2-14), then finds a new view in worship: the end of the wicked, and above all the presence of God as the psalmist's portion (Ps 73:23-26). It does not deny the facts; it changes the frame.

items.title: Habakkuk
items.summary: A prophet who questions God's justice and ends in trust without answers.
items.detail: Habakkuk asks why God tolerates violence in Judah; God says he is raising up Babylon. That makes it worse: how can a holy God use a more wicked nation? The prophet waits on the watchtower and receives the promise that the righteous will live by faithfulness. The book ends with a song of trust even if the fig tree does not blossom (Hab 3:17-19).

items.title: Lamentations
items.summary: Poems of grief after Jerusalem's destruction, with hope at the centre.
items.detail: The book admits Judah's sin but refuses to let that explain away the horror; it describes starving mothers and slaughtered priests (Lam 2:20). Its centre declares that the Lord's mercies are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23) and that he does not afflict from the heart (Lam 3:33). It ends with a question, not an answer. Jews read it on Tisha B'Av, the fast for the temple's fall.

items.title: Ecclesiastes
items.summary: Life 'under the sun' is fleeting; time and chance happen to all.
items.detail: The Teacher observes that the race is not always to the swift and that righteous people perish while the wicked live long (Eccl 7:15, Eccl 9:11). He refuses simple formulas but still counsels fearing God, enjoying God's gifts and remembering judgement (Eccl 12:13-14). The Hebrew word hevel ('vapour, breath') describes life's brevity and elusiveness.

items.title: The tower of Siloam
items.summary: Jesus: those eighteen victims were not worse sinners than anyone else.
items.detail: People tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate. He raises a second case himself, a natural disaster: a tower that fell and killed eighteen. In both cases he denies that the victims were especially guilty, then turns the question back: 'unless you repent, you will all likewise perish'. Disaster is a call to everyone, not a verdict on the victims.

items.title: The man born blind
items.summary: 'Who sinned, this man or his parents?' Neither.
items.detail: The disciples assume a moral cause behind a birth defect, a view found in some Jewish teaching of the time. Jesus rejects both options and says the man's condition is an occasion for 'the works of God' to be displayed, and then heals him. The sentence is about what God will do, not a claim that God blinded him for a show; translators and interpreters debate the exact sense of John 9:3.

items.title: Joseph: meant for evil, meant for good
items.summary: Two intentions in one event: the brothers' evil and God's good purpose.
items.detail: Joseph tells his brothers that they meant to harm him but God meant it for good, to keep many people alive (Gen 50:20). Reformed theologians read this as God ordaining the event; others read it as God redeeming an evil he permitted. Either way the text holds the brothers responsible and does not call the betrayal good.

items.title: Paul's thorn in the flesh
items.summary: A 'messenger of Satan' that God did not remove, through which Christ's power was shown.
items.detail: Paul pleads three times for relief and receives the answer: 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness' (2 Cor 12:9). The text holds together Satan's harm, God's purpose (to keep Paul from pride) and an unanswered request. What the thorn was is unknown.

items.title: Romans 8: groaning and glory
items.summary: Creation, believers and the Spirit all groan toward renewal; nothing separates us from God's love.
items.detail: Paul says creation was 'subjected to futility' in hope and waits for liberation (Rom 8:20-21). Believers groan too, and the Spirit groans in prayer (Rom 8:23-26). Verse 28 says God works in all things for good for those who love him; it does not say all things are good. The chapter ends with a list of real dangers that cannot separate us from God's love (Rom 8:35-39).

items.title: Revelation 21: no more tears
items.summary: The end of the story: God dwells with humans and death is no more.
items.detail: The martyrs ask 'How long?' (Rev 6:10). The book answers with judgement on evil powers and a new heaven and new earth where God wipes every tear and mourning and pain are gone (Rev 21:4). Many theologians say any adequate theodicy must look here, because only the end of the story can show whether evil is truly defeated.

items.title: Augustine of Hippo (354-430)
items.summary: Evil is the absence of good, entered through free will; God brings good out of it.
items.detail: Augustine had been a Manichean, believing in two equal powers of good and evil. He rejected this: God made all things good, and evil is a privation, a lack or corruption of good. Sin began in the free choice of angels and humans, and the disorder of nature followed. His influence on Western theology is enormous. Critics ask how a perfectly good creature could first choose evil, and how a historical Fall fits with suffering in nature long before humans.

items.title: Irenaeus of Lyon (about 130-202)
items.summary: Humans were made as children, to grow into the likeness of God.
items.detail: Irenaeus taught that Adam and Eve were created immature and that God patiently trains humanity toward maturity, with Christ recapitulating (summing up and restoring) the human story. He did not write a full theodicy, but John Hick named the 'Irenaean' type after him. Scholars debate how closely Hick's version matches Irenaeus.

items.title: Leibniz and Voltaire
items.summary: 'The best of all possible worlds' and its famous mockery.
items.detail: Leibniz (1646-1716) argued that God, being perfect, must choose the best possible world, and that the evils in it are part of the best overall whole. After the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Voltaire satirised the idea in *Candide*, whose tutor Pangloss keeps insisting that all is for the best amid disaster. Leibniz's actual argument is more careful than Pangloss, and some modern philosophers still defend a version of it.

items.title: Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov
items.summary: The protest of love against a harmony built on a child's tears.
items.detail: In *The Brothers Karamazov* (1880), Ivan collects true newspaper stories of cruelty to children and says he cannot accept any final harmony that requires them; he respectfully 'returns his ticket'. His brother Alyosha does not refute him with argument but answers with Christ's forgiveness and active love. Many theologians say this chapter is the strongest statement of the problem ever written.

items.title: C. S. Lewis: two books on pain
items.summary: *The Problem of Pain* (1940) argued; *A Grief Observed* (1961) cried out.
items.detail: In 1940 Lewis defended free will, a fallen world and pain as God's 'megaphone to rouse a deaf world'. After the death of his wife Joy Davidman in 1960 he wrote a raw journal, first published under a pseudonym, describing God as a door slammed in his face, before slowly recovering faith. Readers value the pair because they show that the intellectual and personal problems are different.

items.title: John Hick (1922-2012)
items.summary: *Evil and the God of Love* (1966) and the 'vale of soul-making'.
items.detail: Hick argued that God created humans at an 'epistemic distance', in a world where God is not obvious and where real dangers exist, so that faith and moral growth could be free. He borrowed John Keats' phrase 'the vale of soul-making'. To deal with lives cut short, he relied on growth continuing after death and, controversially, on universal salvation.

items.title: Alvin Plantinga (born 1932)
items.summary: *God, Freedom and Evil* (1974): the free-will defence.
items.detail: Plantinga offered a defence, not a theodicy: he did not claim to know God's actual reasons, only to show a possible one. If creatures are significantly free, it is possible that every world God could create with free creatures would contain some evil (he called this 'transworld depravity'). Many philosophers, including atheists, came to accept that the strict logical problem had been answered. He extended the defence to natural evil by suggesting it could be caused by free fallen spirits.

items.title: William Rowe (1931-2015)
items.summary: The fawn in the forest fire and the evidential argument (1979).
items.detail: Rowe, who called himself a 'friendly atheist', granted that theists could be rational. But he argued that intense suffering which seems to serve no good, like a fawn dying slowly and unseen in a fire, makes it likely that pointless evil exists, and so likely that God does not. His argument remains a central point of debate.

items.title: Marilyn McCord Adams (1943-2017)
items.summary: Horrendous evils must be defeated within each life.
items.detail: An Episcopal priest and philosopher, Adams argued in *Horrendous Evils and the Goodness of God* (1999) that it is not enough for God to bring overall good from evil. God must be good to each person who suffered, making their life worth living on the whole, finally through intimate union with God, who in Christ shared horrendous suffering. Her view leans toward universal salvation, which critics question.

items.title: Jürgen Moltmann (1926-2024)
items.summary: *The Crucified God*: God suffers in the cross of Christ.
items.detail: As a German prisoner of war, Moltmann found hope reading Mark's account of Jesus' cry of forsakenness. In *The Crucified God* (1972) he argued that the cross is an event within God: the Father suffers the loss of the Son, the Son suffers abandonment, and the Spirit brings life out of death. Supporters find this deeply consoling; classical theologians worry it makes God dependent on the world.

items.title: Greg Boyd (born 1957)
items.summary: Warfare theodicy: much evil is the work of God's enemies.
items.detail: In *God at War* (1997) and *Satan and the Problem of Evil* (2001), Boyd argues that the Bible's main framework for evil is a cosmic conflict with rebellious powers, and that Jesus' ministry treats sickness and oppression as the work of the enemy. He combines this with open theism. Critics, especially Reformed ones, think he limits God's sovereignty too much.

items.title: Process thinkers
items.summary: God's power is persuasion; God suffers with the world.
items.detail: Alfred North Whitehead (*Process and Reality*, 1929) called God 'the fellow-sufferer who understands'. Charles Hartshorne (*Omnipotence and Other Theological Mistakes*, 1984) and David Ray Griffin (*God, Power, and Evil*, 1976) argued that the classic idea of all-controlling power is incoherent. Thomas Jay Oord's 'essential kenosis' is a related evangelical-leaning view. Critics say this God cannot guarantee the final defeat of evil.

items.title: Elie Wiesel (1928-2016)
items.summary: *Night*: faith wounded at Auschwitz, protest that never let go of God.
items.detail: Wiesel was deported from Sighet at fifteen; his mother, sister and father died in the camps. *Night* describes the hanging of a child and a voice asking where God is, and Wiesel's inner answer that God is there, hanging on the gallows; readers interpret this as the death of faith, as God suffering with victims, or as both. His later play *The Trial of God* puts God on trial. He remained an observant, questioning Jew.

items.title: Emil Fackenheim (1916-2003)
items.summary: The '614th commandment': do not hand Hitler posthumous victories.
items.detail: Fackenheim, a rabbi and philosopher who was himself held in a camp in 1938, said in 1967 that Jews hear a commanding voice from Auschwitz: they must survive as Jews, remember the victims, not despair of the world or of God. The number adds one to the traditional 613 commandments of the Torah. Some Jewish thinkers object that no commandment can be added.

items.title: Rubenstein and Jonas
items.summary: Two radical answers: the God of history is dead; God gave up power.
items.detail: Richard Rubenstein (*After Auschwitz*, 1966) concluded that the traditional God who acts in history and chose Israel could not be believed after the Holocaust, though he valued Jewish community and ritual. Hans Jonas, in 'The Concept of God after Auschwitz' (lecture 1984), proposed that God, in creating, gave up power, so God did not intervene because God could not. Most Jews and Christians reject both, but both take the evil with full seriousness.

items.title: Harold Kushner (1935-2023)
items.summary: *When Bad Things Happen to Good People* (1981).
items.detail: Kushner's son Aaron had progeria and died at fourteen. Kushner read Job as choosing God's goodness over God's total power, and concluded that God does not cause our suffering but helps us bear it. His pastoral wisdom (do not blame the sufferer, do not blame God for a world of natural law) helped many. Critics said a God who cannot help is not the God of the Bible.

items.title: The Lisbon earthquake (1755)
items.summary: The natural disaster that shook the European Enlightenment.
items.detail: On All Saints' Day an earthquake, then a tsunami and fires, destroyed much of Lisbon. Preachers called it judgement; Voltaire asked whether Lisbon was more wicked than Paris or London. Rousseau replied that humans had built crowded tall houses, so not all the harm was natural. The debate began the modern focus on natural evil.

items.title: The 2004 tsunami in Tamil Nadu
items.summary: Natural evil on the Indian coast, and how faith communities responded.
items.detail: The wave of 26 December 2004 killed thousands along the Tamil Nadu coast, many of them fishing families, with Nagapattinam district hit hardest. Some explained it as karma, some as divine judgement, some as nature. Christian, Hindu and Muslim groups worked side by side in relief. The case tests the theodicies: none explain why these villages, and Jesus' words on Siloam warn against reading guilt into victims.

items.title: Amy Carmichael at Dohnavur
items.summary: A missionary in Tamil Nadu who wrote from twenty years of pain.
items.detail: Amy Carmichael (1867-1951) founded the Dohnavur Fellowship in Tamil Nadu to protect children at risk. After a fall in 1931 she was largely bedridden until her death. Her writings from that period, such as *Rose from Brier*, written for fellow sufferers, refuse cheap comfort and speak of accepting what God does not remove while trusting his love.

items.title: Gladys Staines forgives
items.summary: Moral evil and forgiveness in Odisha, 1999.
items.detail: In January 1999 the Australian missionary Graham Staines, who had served leprosy patients in Odisha for decades, was burned to death with his two young sons by a mob. His widow Gladys publicly forgave the killers and continued the work. Her response did not explain the evil; it answered it with forgiveness, a costly act many Indians across faiths found moving.

items.title: Nicholas Wolterstorff, *Lament for a Son*
items.summary: A philosopher's grief after his son's climbing accident (1987).
items.detail: Wolterstorff, a leading Christian philosopher, wrote short meditations after his 25-year-old son Eric died. He refuses to say that God caused it for a reason, and he refuses to give up on God. He writes that he does not know why, and that God, too, suffers. The book is widely used in grief ministry.
