spectrum.title: How directly is God involved in each evil?
spectrum.intro: This line runs from views in which God specifically decrees every event, to views in which God cannot prevent evil at all. Sincere Christians and Jews stand at every point. Most positions near the middle are combinations. Read the positions on the other side as their best defenders would state them.
spectrum.left: God specifically ordains every event, including each evil, for a good purpose
spectrum.right: God cannot prevent evil; God persuades and suffers with the world

stops.label: Meticulous providence
stops.text: Every event, from a falling sparrow to a cancer cell, is ordained by God's decree, and every evil has a specific good purpose. God is not the author of sin because he works through secondary causes and human choices. This view offers the strongest assurance that nothing is wasted.
stops.who: John Calvin; Jonathan Edwards; John Piper; Paul Helm

stops.label: Reformed compatibilism with mystery
stops.text: God ordains all things, and humans are fully responsible, but we cannot explain how these fit together. We should hold both because Scripture teaches both, and refuse to call God evil or make humans puppets.
stops.who: D. A. Carson (*How Long, O Lord?*); Westminster Confession; many Reformed pastors

stops.label: Thomist permission
stops.text: God is the first cause of all being but does not cause evil as such, since evil is a lack, not a thing. God permits evil to bring good from it. God's causation and creaturely freedom are on different levels, so they do not compete.
stops.who: Thomas Aquinas; many Catholic theologians; Brian Davies; Eleonore Stump (in her own form)

stops.label: Molinism (middle knowledge)
stops.text: God knows what every possible free creature would freely do in every situation, and chooses which world to create in light of that. God thus has full providence without determining choices. Evil is permitted as part of the best feasible world of free creatures.
stops.who: Luis de Molina; William Lane Craig; Thomas Flint

stops.label: Free-will theodicy
stops.text: God gave real freedom and so permits evil he does not want. He does not decree each evil, but foresees it and brings good from it. Natural evil follows the Fall or comes from fallen spiritual beings.
stops.who: Augustine (in part); C. S. Lewis; Alvin Plantinga; Richard Swinburne

stops.label: Soul-making
stops.text: God deliberately made a world with dangers and distance so that freedom and growth would be real. God allows evils generally, as features of a good kind of world, not as specific decrees.
stops.who: John Hick; elements in Swinburne and Irenaeus

stops.label: Natural-law theodicy
stops.text: God made a world that runs by stable laws, which we need in order to act responsibly and learn. The same laws that hold life together also produce earthquakes and diseases. God does not usually override them.
stops.who: Richard Swinburne; John Polkinghorne ('free-process defence'); Christopher Southgate on evolution

stops.label: Cosmic conflict
stops.text: God's will is often opposed by real rebel powers. Many evils are acts of war against God, not his plan. God has committed himself to fight by love and the cross, not by overpowering force, until the final victory.
stops.who: Greg Boyd; many early church fathers; Christus Victor tradition

stops.label: Open theism
stops.text: The future is partly open. God takes risks, responds to prayer and choices, and can be grieved. Specific evils are not planned or always foreseen in detail. God is still able to intervene and will finally win.
stops.who: Clark Pinnock; John Sanders; William Hasker; David Basinger

stops.label: Essential kenosis
stops.text: God's nature is self-giving, uncontrolling love. God cannot unilaterally prevent evil, not because of outside limits but because love by its nature does not control. God works with creatures to heal and redeem.

stops.label: Process theology
stops.text: God's power is persuasive by its nature. God offers each moment its best possibility and absorbs the world's suffering into his own life. God cannot stop evil but never stops working against it.
stops.who: Alfred North Whitehead; Charles Hartshorne; David Ray Griffin; John Cobb

stops.label: A God who gave up power
stops.text: In creating, God surrendered power so that the world could be itself. After Auschwitz, we must think of a suffering, becoming, caring, but not all-powerful God. Humans must now help God.
stops.who: Hans Jonas; in a different pastoral form, Harold Kushner

cases.title: Job's friends: when good theology is applied badly
cases.question: Eliphaz says the innocent never perish. What is wrong with that, if the Bible elsewhere says sin brings ruin?

steps.note: 'Who that was innocent ever perished?' (Job 4:7). Those who plough iniquity reap trouble (Job 4:8). It sounds like Proverbs and Deuteronomy.

Eliphaz turns a general pattern into a rule that works backwards: if you suffer, you must have sinned. Bildad applies it even to Job's dead children (Job 8:4), and Zophar says Job deserves worse (Job 11:6).

Job insists he is innocent and calls his friends 'worthless physicians' who 'whitewash with lies' (Job 13:4). He says their silence would be wisdom (Job 13:5). He brings his complaint to God, not to them.
God tells Eliphaz, 'you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has' (Job 42:7). The protester is approved; the defenders of God are rebuked and need Job to pray for them.

cases.takeaway: Defending God by blaming the sufferer is condemned by God himself. True statements about sin and judgement become false when used to explain a particular person's pain.

cases.title: The man born blind: a wrong question replaced
cases.question: When the disciples ask whose sin caused the blindness, what does Jesus change?

steps.note: The disciples assume a moral cause and only ask whose: the man's (perhaps before birth) or his parents'. Some Jewish teaching of the time discussed both possibilities.
'Neither this man nor his parents sinned' (John 9:3). He does not deny that sin exists; he denies that this suffering is a sign of special guilt.

steps.step: Jesus turns from cause to purpose
steps.note: The question moves from 'why did this happen?' to 'what will God do here?'. Jesus says 'we must work the works of him who sent me' (John 9:4), then heals the man.
By the end, the man sees and confesses faith, while the religious leaders who were sure of their theology are called blind (John 9:39-41).

cases.takeaway: Jesus moves the focus from blame to God's healing work. The fitting response to suffering is compassion and action, not a search for the guilty party.

cases.title: Siloam: a disaster is not a verdict
cases.question: What does Jesus teach about a political massacre and an accidental collapse?

steps.note: Pilate killed Galileans while they offered sacrifices (moral evil). A tower fell in Siloam and killed eighteen (an accident, natural evil). Jesus addresses both.
Twice Jesus asks, 'Do you think they were worse?' and answers, 'No' (Luke 13:2-5).
Instead of explaining the deaths, Jesus uses them as a warning to all: life is fragile and judgement is real. The disaster says something to the living, not about the dead.

Luke follows with a parable of patience for a fruitless tree (Luke 13:6-9) and a healing of a woman whom Satan had bound for eighteen years (Luke 13:10-16). God's patience and Jesus' war on evil frame the passage.

cases.takeaway: Christians should not read the tsunami, an earthquake or a bomb as proof of the victims' special guilt. Disasters call everyone to humility and turning to God.

cases.title: Joseph: two intentions in one event
cases.question: How can the same event be meant for evil and meant for good?

steps.note: The brothers planned murder, then sold Joseph into slavery (Gen 37:18-28). Joseph suffered years of slavery and prison.
'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive' (Gen 50:20). The same Hebrew verb is used for both intentions.

Reformed readers see God ordaining the event without being guilty of the brothers' sin. Free-will and open theists read it as God weaving a free evil into a good outcome. All agree the brothers were guilty and God was good.
He weeps, forgives and provides for the brothers (Gen 50:21). His theology leads to mercy, not revenge.

cases.takeaway: Scripture can hold human evil and God's good purpose in one event without calling the evil good. This text comforts many, but it is Joseph's testimony looking back, not a sentence to impose on someone else's fresh grief.

cases.title: Psalm 88: when prayer ends in darkness
cases.question: What do we do with a psalm that never finds comfort?

steps.note: Notice that every complaint is spoken to God. 'O Lord, God of my salvation' (Ps 88:1) is the address of a believer, even when the content is despair.
The psalmist says God's wrath lies on him and God has removed his friends (Ps 88:7-8). He does not blame himself; he puts the weight on God.
'Do you work wonders for the dead?' (Ps 88:10-12). He argues with God from God's own interest in being praised.
The final words are about darkness (Ps 88:18). There is no turn to praise. The psalm stayed in Israel's worship book anyway.

cases.takeaway: Faith sometimes looks like refusing to stop speaking to God when no comfort comes. The church should leave room for people whose prayers sound like Ps 88.

cases.title: Paul's thorn: an unanswered prayer that became a gift
cases.question: Why did God not remove Paul's affliction?

steps.note: The thorn was 'given' to Paul, it is 'a messenger of Satan', and its purpose was to keep him from pride (2 Cor 12:7). Paul sees God's purpose and Satan's harm in one affliction.
He asks plainly for it to go (2 Cor 12:8). Asking for healing is not a lack of faith.
'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness' (2 Cor 12:9).
He chooses to boast in weakness and to be content in hardship 'for the sake of Christ' (2 Cor 12:10). This is the theology of the cross in personal form.

cases.takeaway: Not every suffering is removed, even for great saints. Grace can meet us inside it. Paul's experience corrects any teaching that strong faith always brings healing.

cases.title: The 2004 tsunami: karma, judgement or groaning creation?
cases.question: How should Christians in Tamil Nadu speak about a disaster that killed thousands of fishing families?

steps.note: People asked: Was this karma from past lives? Was it God's punishment? Was it the sea goddess? Before answering, Christians are called to weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15) and help.
Jesus' answer about Siloam applies directly: those who died were not worse than others (Luke 13:4-5). This also answers a strict karma reading that sees the victims as paying for past deeds.
Paul describes a creation 'subjected to futility' and 'groaning' until it is freed (Rom 8:20-22). The disaster is a sign that the world is not yet as God intends, not a message about these villages.

steps.step: Speak of grace and hope respectfully
steps.note: Christians can say that God's love is not earned or lost by past deeds (Ps 103:10), that Jesus shares our suffering, and that God promises renewal. Many Hindu neighbours also believe in divine grace; respectful conversation starts there, not with attacking their faith.

cases.takeaway: Natural disasters are best spoken of as the groaning of an unfinished creation, met by God's presence and his people's help, never as proof that the victims deserved it.

sections.heading: What theodicy is, and what it is not
sections.body:
The word 'theodicy' was made by the philosopher Gottfried Leibniz in 1710 from two Greek words, theos (God) and dike (justice). A theodicy tries to justify the ways of God: to give the actual reasons, or the most likely reasons, why a good and powerful God allows evil. The poet John Milton had already set himself the same aim in *Paradise Lost* (1667): to 'justify the ways of God to men'.

Philosophers distinguish a theodicy from a 'defence'. A defence is more modest. It does not claim to know God's reasons; it only shows that God and evil are not logically contradictory, by describing a possible reason. Alvin Plantinga's free-will defence is the best-known example.

The problem is usually set out as an 'inconsistent triad': (1) God is all-powerful, (2) God is wholly good, (3) evil exists. A good being would want to remove evil; a powerful being could. So why is evil here? Lactantius, a Christian writer of the early fourth century, reports this dilemma from the Greek philosopher Epicurus, and David Hume restated it in 1779 as 'Epicurus's old questions'.

Some theologians criticise the whole project. Kenneth Surin and Terrence Tilley argued that theodicy can turn real victims into examples in an argument and can make evil seem acceptable. Their warning matters: theodicy should never replace lament, justice or care. But most Christian thinkers still believe careful reflection is a form of loving God with the mind, and that believers deserve honest help with honest questions.

callout.text: Three words to keep apart: theodicy (claims to give God's reasons), defence (shows a possible reason, so no contradiction), and lament (speaks to God about evil instead of explaining it). The Bible contains much more lament than theodicy.

sections.heading: The logical problem and the evidential problem
sections.body:
The logical problem says belief in God is self-contradictory. J. L. Mackie's 1955 article 'Evil and Omnipotence' argued this. For it to work, it must be necessarily true that a good, all-powerful God would prevent every evil. Plantinga replied that this is not necessarily true: if God wants creatures who freely choose good, he cannot guarantee that they always will, because a guaranteed free choice is not free. If that is even possible, there is no contradiction. Many philosophers, including well-known atheists, now accept that the logical form of the argument does not succeed.

The evidential problem is different. It grants that God and evil are consistent, but says the facts make God unlikely. William Rowe's 1979 paper asked us to picture a fawn trapped in a forest fire, badly burned, suffering for days and then dying, with no human ever knowing. What good could that serve? If there is even one truly pointless evil, Rowe argued, a perfectly good God does not exist; and it seems very likely that there is such evil.

Replies to Rowe take three main forms. Skeptical theists (Stephen Wykstra, 1984; Michael Bergmann) say we are not in a position to judge that an evil has no purpose, given the gap between God's mind and ours. Others (Peter van Inwagen, William Hasker) argue that a world with real freedom and stable natural laws will contain some pointless evils, and that God may permit them. Still others, especially Reformed thinkers, argue that the overall evidence for God, including the resurrection of Jesus, outweighs the evidence from evil.

There is also a third form, sometimes called the existential or pastoral problem: not 'Does God exist?' but 'How can I trust God after this?'. Arguments rarely help here. This is where lament, community and the cross come first.

callout.text: Whether skeptical theism goes too far is debated. Critics such as Paul Draper and some theists argue that if we cannot judge God's reasons for permitting evil, we also cannot judge that anything is good or bad, or trust God's promises. Defenders reply that we can trust God's revealed promises while admitting we cannot see his reasons for particular evils.

sections.heading: Kinds of evil: moral, natural, gratuitous and horrendous
sections.body:
Moral evil is evil done by agents who could have chosen otherwise: murder, lies, abuse, exploitation, genocide. Natural evil is suffering that comes from the way the natural world works: earthquakes, floods, cancers, birth defects. Many events are mixed. A famine may begin with drought and be made deadly by corruption; an earthquake kills more people where buildings are poorly made.

The Bible attributes moral evil to the human heart and to rebellious spiritual powers (Mark 7:21-23, Eph 6:12). It links natural disorder to the curse after human sin (Gen 3:17-19) and to a creation 'subjected to futility' that waits for freedom (Rom 8:20-21). It also shows God governing wild nature in ways humans cannot judge (Job 38-41), and Jesus treating disease as an enemy to defeat (Luke 13:16, Acts 10:38).

Gratuitous evil means evil that serves no greater good at all. Whether such evil exists is the central question in the evidential debate. Horrendous evil, a term from Marilyn McCord Adams, means evil so terrible that it seems to destroy the value of the victim's whole life. Adams argued that God must not only bring good out of such evil for the world in general, but must make each victim's life a great good to them, and that only intimate union with God can do that.

Naming the kind of evil helps avoid harm. Treating cancer as if it were someone's moral failure, or treating abuse as if it were simply 'nature', causes real damage.

sections.heading: Job: the Bible's great argument about suffering
sections.body:
The book of Job opens in heaven. 'The satan' (in Hebrew ha-satan, 'the accuser', with the definite article) appears among the heavenly beings and asks whether Job serves God for nothing (Job 1:9). Many scholars think this figure is a member of God's council acting as prosecutor, not yet the fully developed devil of later Jewish and Christian thought; others see continuity with the later figure. Either way, the question on trial is whether humans can love God for God's own sake.

Job loses his wealth, children and health. His first response is worship (Job 1:21). Then three friends come and sit with him in silence for seven days (Job 2:13), which is the wisest thing they do. When Job curses the day of his birth (Job 3), they begin to defend God with the theology of retribution: the innocent do not perish, so Job must have sinned. Job refuses this. He demands to argue his case before God (Job 13:3, Job 31:35-37) while still hoping for a redeemer (Job 19:25-27).

God answers 'out of the whirlwind' (Job 38:1). He asks Job where he was when the earth was founded, and shows him the wild animals, the sea, Behemoth and Leviathan, none of which exist for human convenience. God never mentions the heavenly test. Job is humbled and comforted (Job 42:6; the Hebrew of this verse is difficult and can mean 'repent' or 'be comforted' about dust and ashes). Then God says the friends were wrong and Job was right (Job 42:7).

Job's message is complex. It teaches that suffering is not always punishment; that honest protest is welcomed by God more than false defence of him; that God's wisdom governs a world much larger than human concerns; and that the deepest answer is an encounter with God, not an explanation. Jewish tradition read Job as a model of patience and also of protest; Christians have often seen in the innocent sufferer a foreshadowing of Christ.

callout.text: Scholars debate whether the happy ending (Job 42:10-17) supports or weakens the book's challenge to retribution theology, and whether God's speeches are an answer, a rebuke, or a deliberate refusal to answer. Some also read Elihu's speeches (Job 32-37) as a later addition; others see them as preparing for God's speech.

sections.heading: Lament: faith that complains
sections.body:
About a third of the Psalms are laments. They follow a common pattern: address to God, complaint, request, expression of trust, and promise of praise. Walter Brueggemann described the Psalms as moving through orientation (life makes sense), disorientation (life falls apart) and new orientation (surprised by grace). Lament belongs to the middle stage, and the Bible gives it a large share.

In a Jewish covenant setting, lament is not rebellion. It is the speech of a partner who holds God to his promises. Psalm 44 says Israel has been faithful and still been crushed, and calls God to 'wake up'. Psalm 13 asks 'How long?' four times before it can say 'I trust'. Psalm 88 never reaches trust. Lamentations mourns Jerusalem with five careful poems, mixing confession of sin with protest against the horror.

The argument with God runs through the whole Bible. Abraham bargains for Sodom: 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?' (Gen 18:25). Moses stands between God and the people (Exod 32:11-14). Jeremiah accuses God of deceiving him (Jer 20:7). Habakkuk asks why God is silent while the wicked swallow the righteous (Hab 1:13). Jesus prays Psalm 22 on the cross.

Many churches sing almost only praise. Biblical scholars and pastors have argued that this leaves sufferers without words and suggests that complaint is unfaithful. Recovering lament gives people permission to bring their whole selves to God.

callout.text: Myth: complaining to God shows weak faith. In the Bible, the people who complain most honestly to God (Job, Jeremiah, the psalmists, Jesus in Gethsemane) are those closest to him. The opposite of lament is not faith; it is silence and distance.

sections.heading: Jesus, the cross and the God who suffers
sections.body:
Jesus did not give a theory of evil. He refused to blame victims (Luke 13:1-5, John 9:1-3), healed the sick and freed the oppressed as signs that God's kingdom was breaking in, and called evil by its name. He wept at Lazarus' tomb even though he was about to raise him (John 11:35). In Gethsemane he asked for the cup to pass (Mark 14:36).

On the cross, the innocent one suffers the worst of moral evil: betrayal, injustice, torture, mockery, and the feeling of abandonment by God (Mark 15:34). The New Testament says this was done by 'lawless men' and also happened 'according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God' (Acts 2:23). It is the clearest example of God bringing the greatest good, salvation, out of the greatest evil, without calling the evil good.

Martin Luther's 'theology of the cross' (Heidelberg Disputation, 1518) says God is found especially in suffering and weakness. Jürgen Moltmann (*The Crucified God*, 1972) went further: God himself suffers in the cross. The early church held that God is impassible (not subject to suffering as creatures are), and taught that the Son suffered in his human nature. Many modern theologians believe God truly feels grief, pointing to texts such as Gen 6:6, Hos 11:8 and Isa 63:9. Paul Gavrilyuk and others have argued that the Fathers' position was more subtle than its critics say: God freely and truly enters suffering in Christ without being overcome by it.

The cross is also a victory. The tradition called Christus Victor, named by Gustaf Aulén in 1930, stresses that at the cross Christ disarmed the powers (Col 2:15) and destroyed the one who has the power of death (Heb 2:14). The resurrection is God's announcement that evil and death will not have the last word.

callout.text: Passibility (God can suffer) and impassibility (God is not subject to suffering) is a live debate. Both sides agree that in Jesus, God truly entered human suffering. They disagree about whether the divine nature itself is changed by it.

sections.heading: The main Christian responses in brief
sections.body:
The Augustinian response: creation was very good; evil is the absence or corruption of good; it came through the free rebellion of angels and humans; natural disorder followed the Fall; God permits evil to bring greater good from it. Free-will defences and theodicies (Plantinga, Swinburne) develop this tradition.

The Irenaean or soul-making response (John Hick): humans were created immature, at a distance from God, in a world of challenge, so that they could freely grow into the likeness of God. Suffering is the price of a world in which courage, compassion and faith are possible.

The Reformed response: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, as the Westminster Confession (1646) puts it, yet is not the author of sin and does not remove human responsibility. Evil is never meaningless. Gen 50:20 and Acts 4:27-28 are central. Greater-good theodicies (God permits or ordains evil only for an outweighing good) are found here and in many other traditions.

The cosmic-conflict response: creation is a war zone between God and rebel spiritual powers; much evil is the enemy's work; Jesus came to destroy the works of the devil. Open theism adds that the future is partly open, so God does not plan each evil. Natural-law theodicy (Swinburne, Polkinghorne) says a world of stable laws, needed for responsible action, will also produce disasters. Process theology says God's power is persuasive, not coercive.

Finally, the 'best of all possible worlds' view (Leibniz) says that God chose the best whole, evils included. Skeptical theism is less a theodicy than a reason not to expect one. Most believers combine several of these, for example free will for moral evil, natural law or cosmic conflict for natural evil, the cross for God's presence, and new creation for final hope.

callout.text: Ask of any response: What does it say about God's power, God's goodness and God's knowledge? What does it say about natural evil? What would it sound like at a child's funeral? A theodicy that cannot be said at a funeral may still be true, but it should be said with great care.

sections.heading: Jewish voices: covenant, protest and the Holocaust
sections.body:
Jewish tradition reads suffering within the covenant. Deuteronomy links blessing and curse to faithfulness (Deut 28), and the prophets read the exile as judgement. But the same Scriptures contain Job, Ecclesiastes and the lament psalms, which deny that all suffering is punishment. The rabbis spoke of 'sufferings of love' (yissurin shel ahavah) and also told stories in which they argued with God. Hasidic tradition remembers Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev bringing 'a lawsuit' against God on behalf of Israel.

The Holocaust (the Shoah) shook all of this. Six million Jews, including about one and a half million children, were murdered. Richard Rubenstein (*After Auschwitz*, 1966) said the God who acts in history to save his chosen people could no longer be believed. Emil Fackenheim (1967) replied with the '614th commandment': Jews are forbidden to give Hitler posthumous victories by abandoning Judaism, the Jewish people or hope. Eliezer Berkovits (*Faith after the Holocaust*, 1973) used the biblical idea of hester panim, God hiding his face (Deut 31:17-18, Isa 45:15), and the cost of human freedom. Irving Greenberg proposed that no statement about God should be made that would not be believable in the presence of burning children. Hans Jonas (1984) proposed that God had given up power in creating.

Elie Wiesel's *Night* and his play *The Trial of God* hold faith and protest together: one can put God on trial and still pray afterwards. Harold Kushner's popular book (1981) concluded that God is good but not all-powerful. Most traditional Jewish thinkers rejected that limitation, but many valued his refusal to blame victims.

For Christians, these voices are a gift and a warning. They show that protest can be a form of faith, and they remind Christians of the long history of Christian anti-Judaism that helped prepare the ground for the Holocaust. Christian theodicy must be able to stand in front of Jewish suffering without explaining it away.

callout.text: The phrase 'sufferings of love' comes from the Talmud (Berakhot 5a), where the rabbis discuss suffering that does not come from sin. The discussion that follows (Berakhot 5b) also shows rabbis who said, in effect, 'neither the sufferings nor their reward', preferring to be spared both. Jewish tradition does not give one answer.

sections.heading: Related problems: hiddenness, hell, Old Testament violence and animal pain
sections.body:
Divine hiddenness: J. L. Schellenberg (*Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason*, 1993) argued that a perfectly loving God would make a relationship with himself available to every person who is not resisting it, so the existence of sincere non-believers counts against God. Responses say God hides to protect freedom, to invite seeking, or to deepen trust; the Bible itself speaks of God hiding (Isa 45:15) and of seekers finding (Jer 29:13). The lament 'Why do you hide your face?' (Ps 44:24) shows that believers feel hiddenness too.

Hell: if God allows suffering now for good purposes, what of suffering without end? For many people the problem of hell is the hardest form of the problem of evil. Christians hold three main views: eternal conscious punishment, conditional immortality (the wicked finally perish), and hopeful or Christian universalism. The app's [Afterlife and Kingdom](/afterlife) section sets these out fairly.

Old Testament violence: commands to destroy whole peoples (Deut 20:16-18, 1 Sam 15:3) raise the question of whether God himself commands evil. Responses include ancient war language as hyperbole, God's judgement on specific sins, accommodation to a violent culture, and reading the Old Testament through Jesus. The course lesson [Hard Texts](/course/hard-texts) covers this in detail.

Animal suffering and pre-human evil: fossils show predation, disease and mass extinctions over hundreds of millions of years before humans. This challenges the view that all natural evil follows human sin. Responses include a fall of angelic powers before human history (C. S. Lewis, Plantinga, Boyd), evolutionary theodicy in which a self-making creation is the only way to produce life like ours (Christopher Southgate), and the view that animal death was part of God's good creation while human death is the 'death' brought by sin (Ps 104:21, Job 38:39-41). All look to a renewed creation in which the wolf lies with the lamb (Isa 11:6-9).

sections.heading: Karma, grace and suffering in an Indian setting
sections.body:
Many people in India, including many Christians' neighbours and relatives, explain suffering through karma: actions in this life or past lives bear fruit in later experience. The idea has moral power: it takes responsibility seriously and gives a sense of order. In Tamil tradition the Tirukkural devotes a chapter to destiny (oozh), and Tamil Saiva Siddhanta speaks of souls bound by karma and freed by the grace (arul) of God. Christians should describe these beliefs accurately and respectfully, and should know that grace is a strong theme in Hindu devotion too.

The Bible shares the idea that actions have consequences (Gal 6:7). But it rejects the reverse reasoning that a person's suffering shows what they deserve. Job's friends used that reasoning and were rebuked; Jesus rejected it about the man born blind and the victims at Siloam. A strict karma reading of suffering faces the same problem as the friends' theology: it can make victims of disability, caste oppression or disaster seem to deserve their lot. Dalit Christian theologians such as Arvind Nirmal have stressed that God in Christ stands with the oppressed rather than explaining their suffering as deserved.

The Christian alternative is grace. God 'does not deal with us according to our sins' (Ps 103:10). Salvation is a gift, not earned (Eph 2:8-9). Suffering is part of a creation that groans for renewal, not a ledger of debts. And God himself enters suffering in Jesus. This does not answer every question, but it changes the posture: from 'what did they do?' to 'how can we help, and where is God here?'.

Indian Christian history also has examples of costly response to evil: Amy Carmichael's long illness at Dohnavur, the forgiveness of Gladys Staines in Odisha in 1999, and the shared relief work after the 2004 tsunami. These are not arguments, but they are part of the answer the church gives.

callout.text: In conversation with Hindu friends, avoid caricature. Many Hindu traditions teach grace, devotion (bhakti) and divine compassion. A fruitful question is: 'How does God's grace relate to karma in your tradition?' Then share how Jesus answers the man born blind.

sections.heading: Pastoral wisdom: presence before explanation
sections.body:
When people suffer, they usually need presence before explanations. Job's friends were best in their seven days of silence (Job 2:13). Paul tells us to weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). Jesus wept with Mary and Martha before he did anything else (John 11:33-35).

Things that help: being there, practical help (food, rides, childcare), listening without correcting, reading lament psalms together, praying honestly, remembering anniversaries, and letting people say angry things to God. Things that harm: 'everything happens for a reason', 'God needed another angel', 'if you had more faith', 'at least...', comparing their suffering with others, and pressing Rom 8:28 on fresh grief.

Pastoral theologians such as John Swinton (*Raging with Compassion*, 2007) argue that the church's answer to evil is a set of practices, not a theory: lament, forgiveness, hospitality, thoughtful presence and hope. Nicholas Wolterstorff, after his son's death, wrote that he could not fit the death into any explanation, and that the people who helped were those who simply said they were with him in it.

Theodicy is still useful. People in calm seasons need to think through these questions so that suffering does not find them unprepared, and some sufferers do want to talk about ideas. The wise rule is to let the sufferer lead, and to hold the arguments loosely and the person closely.

callout.text: Myth: Christians must always have an answer. Scripture itself leaves many 'why' questions open (Deut 29:29). Saying 'I do not know why, but I am here and God has not left you' is often the most faithful thing a believer can say.

Debate: Is God's justice retributive, restorative, or both?

misreadings.popular: Every event, including every tragedy, has a specific purpose that God planned, so we should accept it and look for the lesson. Saying this is meant to comfort: nothing is random or wasted.
misreadings.inContext: The Bible does affirm God's providence (Gen 50:20, Rom 8:28), but it also shows God grieving over evil (Gen 6:6), Jesus treating sickness and death as enemies (Luke 13:16, John 11:33-35), and the Teacher saying 'time and chance happen to them all' (Eccl 9:11). The phrase as popularly used often slides into fatalism: accept whatever happens because it was meant to be. That is closer to Stoic or popular karma ideas than to the biblical picture of God fighting evil and calling his people to resist it.
misreadings.defence: Reformed scholars such as D. A. Carson and John Piper defend the core truth: God is sovereign over all things, and nothing is outside his purpose. But they also insist that this does not make evil good, does not remove human responsibility, and must not be used as a slogan to silence grief. Carson's *How Long, O Lord?* gives as much space to lament as to sovereignty.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Said to a grieving parent, 'everything happens for a reason' can sound like 'God wanted your child to die'. Even where the theology behind it is held, the phrase is a poor pastoral tool and can drive people from God.

misreadings.popular: If something bad happens to you, God is probably punishing you or warning you about hidden sin. Health and success show God's favour; disaster shows his displeasure.
misreadings.inContext: This is the theology of Job's friends, and God says they did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7). Jesus rejects it for the man born blind (John 9:1-3) and for the victims at Siloam (Luke 13:1-5). Deuteronomy's blessings and curses (Deut 28) are covenant terms for the nation as a whole, not a rule for reading each person's illness or loss. Psalm 44 and Ecclesiastes openly say that the faithful sometimes suffer and the wicked prosper.
misreadings.defence: Traditional scholars note that the Bible does sometimes link a specific suffering to sin (1 Cor 11:29-30, John 5:14), and that sin does bring natural consequences (Gal 6:7). So it is not wrong to examine oneself. The error is making this a universal rule and applying it to other people.
misreadings.whyItMatters: This misreading adds guilt and shame to pain, isolates sufferers, and blames victims of abuse, disability or disaster. It is also the shape of a strict karma reading, so correcting it matters in India.

misreadings.popular: 'All things work together for good' means that whatever happens to a Christian is good, or will soon turn out well in this life.
misreadings.inContext: Paul says God works in all things for good for those who love him, who are called according to his purpose (Rom 8:28). In context, the 'good' is being conformed to the image of Christ (Rom 8:29) and final glory (Rom 8:18, Rom 8:30). The surrounding verses list real evils: groaning creation, weakness, tribulation, famine, sword (Rom 8:22-23, Rom 8:35-36). Paul does not call these good; he says they cannot separate believers from God's love. Some manuscripts read 'God works all things for good', which makes God's action even clearer.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical commentators such as Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner affirm a strong reading of providence here: God really does govern all things toward his people's ultimate good. But they agree that the good is ultimate and Christ-shaped, not necessarily visible or comfortable now.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Used as a quick fix, Rom 8:28 can deny people the right to grieve and make God seem to call evil good. Read in context, it is a deep hope spoken in the middle of groaning.

misreadings.topic: 'If you had enough faith, you would be healed'
misreadings.popular: God always wants to heal and prosper his children. If healing or blessing does not come, the problem is a lack of faith, unconfessed sin or negative words.
misreadings.inContext: Jesus did heal many and connected faith with healing (Mark 5:34). But Paul left Trophimus sick (2 Tim 4:20), told Timothy to take wine for frequent illness (1 Tim 5:23), and was not freed from his thorn (2 Cor 12:7-10). Hebrews lists faithful people who were tortured and killed and 'did not receive what was promised' (Heb 11:35-40). Faith in the Bible includes trust when healing does not come (Hab 3:17-19, Dan 3:17-18).
misreadings.defence: Pentecostal and charismatic teachers rightly stress that God still heals and that prayer for healing is biblical (Jas 5:14-16). Careful leaders in these movements, such as Gordon Fee (himself Pentecostal), criticised prosperity teaching while defending prayer for healing. The healthy view prays boldly and accepts God's answer.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Blaming the sick for their illness adds spiritual abuse to physical suffering. It also makes faith a technique and God a vending machine, which is the opposite of Job's faith that serves God 'for nothing' (Job 1:9).

misreadings.topic: God needs evil to bring about good
misreadings.popular: Good cannot exist without evil, like light without darkness; so God needed evil in order to show his goodness, mercy and justice.
misreadings.inContext: The Bible describes a good creation before evil (Gen 1:31) and a new creation after it (Rev 21:4); evil is an intruder, not a necessary part of reality. God brings good out of evil (Gen 50:20, Rom 5:20), but that is redemption, not dependence. Augustine taught that evil is parasitic on good, not its necessary opposite. The 'light needs darkness' idea is closer to philosophical dualism than to the biblical story.
misreadings.defence: Some Reformed theologians (for example in supralapsarian forms of Calvinism) do say God decreed the Fall so that his mercy and justice could be displayed, and point to Rom 9:22-23. Even they deny that God depends on evil or that evil is good in itself. Other traditions reject this reasoning as making God the author of evil.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If God needs evil, then evil is part of God's own nature or plan in a way that makes him less than wholly good. Keeping evil as an intruder lets believers oppose it wholeheartedly.

misreadings.topic: Lament shows a lack of faith
misreadings.popular: Mature Christians do not complain; they praise God in everything. Questioning God is rebellion or doubt.
misreadings.inContext: The Psalms are Israel's prayer book, and lament is its most common type. Abraham, Moses, Job, Jeremiah and Habakkuk argued with God and were not condemned for it. Jesus himself prayed Psalm 22. In a covenant relationship, complaint addressed to God assumes that God is listening and is bound by his promises. The 'grumbling' condemned in the wilderness (Num 14:1-4) was complaint against God to others, with a wish to go back to Egypt, not lament addressed to God.
misreadings.defence: Scholars from all traditions agree on the place of lament. Some pastors warn rightly that lament should not become permanent bitterness or self-pity, and that the Psalms usually move toward trust. Both concerns can be held together.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Forbidding lament teaches sufferers to hide their pain from God and the church. Restoring it lets faith survive suffering.

misreadings.topic: Theodicy is only an intellectual puzzle
misreadings.popular: The problem of evil is a logic problem for philosophers. Once you have the right argument, the problem is solved.
misreadings.inContext: In the Bible, the problem of evil is mostly faced in prayer, protest, prophecy and action. Job's friends had arguments and were rebuked; Job had questions and met God. The New Testament answer is a person and a story (the cross, the resurrection, the new creation) more than a proof. Theologians such as Kenneth Surin and John Swinton warn that purely abstract theodicy can treat real victims as data.
misreadings.defence: Philosophers of religion such as Plantinga and Swinburne reply that intellectual answers are valuable: they remove false reasons for unbelief and help people think clearly before crisis comes. Their work was never meant to replace pastoral care.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Treating evil only as a puzzle can make Christians cold or glib. Ignoring the intellectual side can leave honest questioners without help. The church needs both, in the right order.

misreadings.topic: The satan in Job is a rival god who controls the world
misreadings.popular: Job shows Satan as a power nearly equal to God, who can do whatever he wants to believers, or alternatively, it shows God making a bet at a human's expense.
misreadings.inContext: In Job, 'the satan' is one of the heavenly beings presenting themselves before God, acting as an accuser. He can act only within limits God sets (Job 1:12, Job 2:6). The scene shows that human suffering is part of a larger story that the sufferer cannot see, not that God plays games. The book never lets Job learn about the scene, which is part of its point.
misreadings.defence: Traditional readers see continuity with the later, fully developed Satan of the New Testament (Rev 12:9-10 calls him the accuser), and warfare theologians stress that real hostile powers exist. Both agree that Job places all such powers under God's ultimate authority.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Overrating the satan leads to dualism and fear; reading the prologue as a cruel bet can make God seem a gambler. The text's restraint keeps the focus on whether faith can be free and on God's final authority.

views.name: Augustinian (privation and Fall)
views.who: Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, much Catholic and Protestant tradition, C. S. Lewis
views.summary: God created everything good. Evil is not a substance but a privation, a lack or twisting of good. It entered through the free rebellion of angels and humans, and nature's disorder followed. God permits evil because he can bring greater good from it, supremely in Christ.
views.strengths: Keeps God wholly good and evil wholly alien; takes human responsibility seriously; has deep roots in Scripture and tradition; explains why evil is parasitic on good.
views.critiques: Struggles to explain how good creatures first chose evil, and how suffering among animals for millions of years can follow human sin. Critics say 'privation' does not capture how active and powerful evil feels.

views.name: Irenaean / soul-making
views.who: Irenaeus (roots), John Hick, Richard Swinburne (in part)
views.summary: Humans were made immature and at an 'epistemic distance' from God in a demanding world, so that they could freely grow into mature children of God. Pain and danger make courage, compassion, patience and trust possible.
views.strengths: Explains why the world is hard rather than a paradise; fits biblical themes of testing and growth (Jas 1:2-4, Rom 5:3-5); looks forward rather than backward.
views.critiques: Much suffering crushes rather than builds character; infants and animals suffer without growing. Hick's dependence on growth after death and universal salvation is disputed. It can make God seem to use people as means.

views.name: Free-will defence and theodicy
views.who: Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne, William Hasker, many evangelical philosophers
views.summary: A world with creatures who are significantly free is more valuable than a world of automatons, and genuine freedom includes the possibility of evil. It is possible that God could not create a world of free beings who never did wrong. This answers the logical problem and explains much moral evil.
views.strengths: Widely accepted as defeating the strict logical problem; fits the biblical call to choose (Deut 30:19); keeps evil as the creature's responsibility.
views.critiques: Does not easily explain natural evil without appeal to fallen spirits. Critics ask why God does not intervene more often, and how this fits with heaven, where the redeemed are free yet do not sin. Reformed critics say it relies on a libertarian view of freedom the Bible does not teach.

views.name: Reformed / meticulous sovereignty
views.who: John Calvin, Jonathan Edwards, Westminster Confession, D. A. Carson, John Piper, Paul Helm
views.summary: God ordains all that comes to pass, including evil acts, without being the author of sin, and humans are fully responsible (compatibilism). Every evil serves God's wise and good purpose, as at the cross (Acts 4:27-28) and in Joseph's story (Gen 50:20).
views.strengths: Takes the Bible's strong providence texts at face value; offers deep assurance that no suffering is meaningless; honours God's glory and freedom.
views.critiques: Many find it hard to see how God is not responsible for evil he decrees. It can sound cold to victims of abuse. Critics say it struggles with texts showing God's grief and opposition to evil.

views.name: Cosmic conflict / warfare
views.who: Many early church fathers, Gustaf Aulén (Christus Victor), Greg Boyd ('trinitarian warfare' model), many Pentecostal and majority-world Christians
views.summary: The world is a war zone. Rebellious spiritual powers, freely created by God, oppress creation and humanity. Much evil is not God's will but the enemy's work. Jesus' healings and exorcisms are acts of war, and the cross is the decisive victory, to be completed at his return.
views.strengths: Matches Jesus' ministry and the New Testament's language of powers; lets believers call particular evils 'not God's will'; makes sense to many cultures that experience spiritual oppression.
views.critiques: Difficult to verify; can make Satan seem too powerful or become an excuse for avoiding human responsibility. Reformed critics say it weakens God's sovereignty; scientists question it as an explanation of natural evil.

views.name: Skeptical theism
views.who: Stephen Wykstra, Michael Bergmann, Daniel Howard-Snyder, many Christian philosophers
views.summary: Given the vast difference between God's knowledge and ours, we should not expect to see God's reasons for allowing many evils. So the fact that some evils look pointless is weak evidence that they are pointless.
views.strengths: Modest and difficult to refute; matches God's answer to Job (Job 38-41) and Isa 55:8-9; can be combined with other views.
views.critiques: Critics say it undermines moral judgement and the reliability of God's promises, and offers little comfort. Some say it would also stop us from inferring God's goodness from the world.

views.name: Open theism
views.who: Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, William Hasker, David Basinger, Greg Boyd
views.summary: God knows all that can be known, but future free choices are not yet settled facts. God takes risks, responds to prayer and can be grieved. Specific evils are not planned and some are pointless, though God works to redeem them.
views.strengths: Takes seriously texts where God changes his mind or is surprised (Gen 6:6, Jer 3:7); frees God from responsibility for specific horrors; supports a relational view of prayer.
views.critiques: Most traditions see it as denying God's full foreknowledge, which Scripture affirms in prophecy (Isa 46:9-10). Critics ask whether God's final victory is secure, and why God, if he can intervene, does not do so more often.

views.name: Process theology
views.who: Alfred North Whitehead, Charles Hartshorne, David Ray Griffin, John Cobb; related: Thomas Jay Oord
views.summary: God's power is persuasive, not coercive. Every creature has some self-determination. God offers each moment its best possibility and suffers with the world, but cannot unilaterally prevent evil.
views.strengths: Removes the question 'why did God not stop it?'; presents God as the fellow-sufferer; fits a scientific picture of an evolving world.
views.critiques: Gives up creation out of nothing and God's power to guarantee the final defeat of evil. Most Christians and Jews judge that it no longer describes the God of the Bible, who raised Jesus from the dead.

views.name: Theology of the cross (cruciform response)
views.who: Martin Luther, Jürgen Moltmann, Kazoh Kitamori, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, many liberation theologians
views.summary: God does not answer suffering from outside but enters it in the crucified Christ. God is known in weakness and godforsakenness. The cross shows God's solidarity with every victim, and the resurrection is God's promise that suffering will not have the last word.
views.strengths: Centres on Jesus; offers deep comfort to victims; refuses easy explanations; joins theodicy to discipleship and solidarity with the oppressed.
views.critiques: Classical theologians worry that some versions make God dependent on the world's suffering. Others note it says how God responds to evil but not why God permits it.

views.name: Jewish protest and post-Holocaust responses
views.who: The biblical lament tradition; Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev; Elie Wiesel; Emil Fackenheim; Eliezer Berkovits; Irving Greenberg; Hans Jonas; Harold Kushner
views.summary: A range of responses rooted in covenant: arguing with God on the basis of his own justice, refusing to let suffering destroy Jewish life and hope, speaking of God hiding his face, and in some cases rethinking God's power. Protest is treated as a form of faithfulness.
views.strengths: Deeply biblical (Abraham, Moses, Job, the Psalms); refuses to explain away horror; keeps faith and honesty together; shaped by the most terrible evidence.
views.critiques: Some forms (Rubenstein, Jonas, Kushner) give up the traditional God, which most Jews and Christians reject. Others leave the question unanswered, which some find unsatisfying, though its defenders see that as honesty.

practice.title: Write your own lament psalm
steps: Read Ps 13 aloud and notice its parts: address, complaint, request, trust, praise.
Choose one real pain in your life or in the world.
Write a few lines for each part. Be honest in the complaint; do not soften it.
If you cannot honestly write the trust or praise lines yet, leave them blank, as Ps 88 does.
Pray it aloud, alone or with one trusted friend.

practice.title: Read Job in one sitting (group exercise)
steps: Divide the book among readers: prologue (Job 1-2), Job's curse (Job 3), sample speeches of Eliphaz (Job 4-5) and Job (Job 6-7), Job's final defence (Job 29-31), God's speeches (Job 38-41), and the ending (Job 42).
Read it aloud as a drama, with different voices for each character.
Discuss: What did the friends get wrong? What did Job get right? Why does God not explain the prologue?
Ask each person to name one time they acted like Job's friends toward someone in pain.

practice.title: Map your own theodicy
steps: Take the decision tree on this page and note which result you reach.
Look up that view in the comparison table. Write down its main strength and main critique.
Read the view furthest from yours on the spectrum, and write its best argument in one paragraph as its defenders would.
Note one place where you need to say 'I do not know'.
Share your map with a friend who holds a different view and listen without arguing.

practice.title: Practise what to say and not to say
steps: In a group, list phrases people said to you or others in times of grief, sorting them into 'helped' and 'hurt'.
Compare the 'hurt' list with the misreadings on this page. Which ones repeat Job's friends?
Write three sentences you could say to someone grieving that are true, kind and do not explain too much (for example, 'I am so sorry. I am here.').
Agree on one practical act of help (a meal, a visit, a call) for someone in your community who is suffering.

practice.title: Read Luke 13 and John 9 against karma and retribution
steps: Read Luke 13:1-5 and John 9:1-7 slowly.
List the assumptions behind the questions people ask Jesus.
Write down how Jesus answers and what he does next.
Discuss respectfully how these passages relate to ideas of karma common in India, and to 'prosperity' preaching in some churches.
Plan how you might explain Jesus' answer gently to a neighbour of another faith.

practice.title: Hope practice with Romans 8
steps: Read Rom 8:18-39 each day for a week.
Each day note one 'groaning' you see in the world or in yourself (Rom 8:22-23).
Then note one sign of hope: an act of love, a small healing, a promise of God.
At the end of the week, read Rev 21:1-5 and write a short prayer for the day when tears are wiped away.
Ask: how does this hope change what I do for people suffering now?
